title: How Isolation Is Actually Enforced — the blocking checks

questions.prompt: In a worktree session you ask Claude to run `cd ../repo && git commit -am wip` to commit work into the main checkout. What stops it?
options: Nothing; only Edit and Write are checked, so Bash git commands pass through
The working-directory and git-redirect checks block it
The file-edit check blocks it because a commit writes files
The command-shape check blocks any `cd` when inside a worktree
questions.explanation: The directory resolves into the main checkout, and the `cd` before git is a redirect into the main checkout — two of the four checks, and the command is blocked. Bash git commands are checked, not exempt. The file-edit check governs `Edit`/`Write`/`NotebookEdit` calls, not a commit run through Bash. The shape check fires when the command text can't be read, not for every `cd`.

questions.prompt: You add a bold rule to CLAUDE.md: "never edit the main checkout from this worktree." Then an agent edits it anyway. What does that tell you about the rule?
options: The rule is enforced by the harness and the agent somehow bypassed a check
The rule was a request the model could decline; only the harness checks are impossible to talk past
CLAUDE.md rules don't load in worktree sessions
The edit must have gone through an MCP tool the checks don't cover
questions.explanation: A written rule is a request the model can reason around; an edit to the main checkout is supposed to be blocked by the file-edit check whether or not any rule exists. If the edit succeeded, the rule wasn't the guard — and the fix is a hook or tool restriction, not a firmer sentence. CLAUDE.md does load (with worktree read-through exceptions for untracked dirs), and MCP tools don't dodge the checks.

questions.prompt: A `cp` command copies a file from a worktree into the main checkout. The isolation checks don't refuse it. Why?
options: The checks only run on the main checkout, not inside worktrees
The checks read the target path, the working directory, and the command text — they don't track which files a shell command writes
The checks only apply to the file-edit tools and never to Bash
questions.explanation: The gap is real and specific: the checks reason about an edit's target path, a command's working directory, and the command text — not about arbitrary filesystem writes a command performs. So a `cp` or shell redirect that never invokes git isn't refused by them; it falls under permissions and sandboxing. The checks do apply to Bash commands, and start on every isolated session.

questions.prompt: A worktree session spawns a subagent. You want to be sure the isolation checks apply to that subagent's edits too. What is true?
options: The checks cover every subagent the isolated session spawns, including one in its own worktree
Only the main session is checked; subagents run with your full permissions
Subagents are checked only if they set `isolation: worktree` themselves
The checks apply to subagents only in the background, not the foreground
questions.explanation: The enforcement follows the isolated session to every subagent it spawns, foreground or background, and also to a subagent that runs in its own worktree. They don't need `isolation: worktree` to be covered. Option B is the false claim this lesson exists to kill; option D inverts the background/foreground detail.
